Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Friday, 15 November 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 060)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Hilbert Chiu SC with Ms Joanna Davidson for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
DR WATERHOUSE: Good morning, Commissioner.
Today we'll be hearing from the third clinician panel
and this panel will consider the issue of patients who no
longer need acute hospital care but cannot be discharged
because of barriers in obtaining the aged care or
disability supports that they need.
The Inquiry has been told that this is a common
scenario with impacts on the patients themselves, the staff
involved in caring for them and bed flows throughout the
system, with the result that other patients or potential
patients can also be affected.
Many of the obstacles are seen as beyond control of
the local health districts and reflect challenges with
Commonwealth Government funded aged care facilities and the
National Disability Insurance Scheme.
That said, there are innovative approaches being taken
to manage local situations to the extent possible.
We have six clinicians participating in this panel
today. In the room with us, there is Amy Okulicz, who is
the nurse unit manager, rehabilitation and geriatric
rehabilitation unit at Wyong Hospital, Central Coast;
Melissa Pickering, the acting director of nursing and
midwifery at Central Coast Local Health District; Brendan
Shortis, acting nurse manager, community health, at Nepean
Blue Mountains,Local Health District.
Giving evidence online, via AVL, all from the
Illawarra Shoalhaven Local Health District, we have
Professor Jan Potter, who is a staff specialist
geriatrician and co-director of aged care and
rehabilitation division for the district; Rachael Hawkins,
the aged care nurse unit manager at Wollongong Hospital;
and Ben Wakeling, director of clinical strategy and
outcomes at the Illawarra Shoalhaven Local Health District.
Commissioner, I'm told that Rachael Hawkins and
Professor Potter will be giving evidence under the oath and
the remaining four witnesses will take an affirmation.

<JAN POTTER, sworn: [10.03am]
<RACHAEL HAWKINS sworn:
<AMY OKULICZ, affirmed:
<MELISSA PICKERING, affirmed:
<BRENDAN JOHN SHORTIS, affirmed:
<BENJAMIN WAKELING, affirmed:
<EXAMINATION BY MS WATERHOUSE:
DR WATERHOUSE: As there are three witnesses in the court
and three online, I'm going to divide this into five broad
topics so that you don't need to try to cover everything
you might like to say in the first couple of answers to
questions that might be asked.
The topics that we'll be covering today are: the
causes of the delays in discharging aged care and NDIS
patients; the effects on bed flow; the consequences and
risks for patients; the impacts on staff; and the actions
taken and other possible solutions to these sorts of
issues.
To start with, though, I'd like to get a sense of the
magnitude of the problem in your respective local health
districts. Could I go to you first, Ms Pickering.
I beg your pardon, I haven't actually got you to state
your full names for the record.
Ms Okulicz, could you state your full name for the
record.
MS OKULICZ: Amy Okulicz.
DR WATERHOUSE: Ms Pickering.
MS PICKERING: Melissa Pickering
DR WATERHOUSE: Mr Shortis.
MS PICKERING: Brendan John Shortis,

DR WATERHOUSE: Professor Potter, could you state your
full name for the record.
MS POTTER: Jan Potter.
MS WATERHOUSE: Ms Hawkins.
MS HAWKINS: Rachael Hawkins.
DR WATERHOUSE: And Mr Wakeling.
MR WAKELING: Benjamin Wakeling.
THE COMMISSIONER: I should just say that if Dr Waterhouse
addresses a particular question to any of you, the rest of
you should feel free to indicate, by any reasonable means,
that you would like to supplement the answer or provide
anything further. So please don't hesitate to jump in as
appropriate.
DR WATERHOUSE: Ms Pickering, if I can go to you, can you
tell me an estimate of how many geriatric and NDIS patients
you have in Central Coast Local Health District facilities
that are waiting there, not requiring acute care but just
waiting for other reasons at the moment.
MS PICKERING: If I can start with the older population
that are sitting across Gosford --
MS WATERHOUSE: I might just get you to move the
microphone a little closer to you.
THE COMMISSIONER: All of you will need to keep your
voices up, mainly for my benefit but also for others.
MS PICKERING: Thank you. In response to the older people
that are sitting within our hospitals on the Central Coast,
across Gosford and Wyong, I guess, on average, if I was to
look at some of the data, September and October this year,
we had between 60 and 70 older people awaiting residential
aged care facility placement. And that's from the time of
assessment to then time of placement, on average, the older
people are in hospital for about two weeks for many
reasons. Some of those reasons include family choosing
a facility for their loved one, and often they will decline
residential aged care facilities until they reach
a facility that they feel is comfortable.

DR WATERHOUSE: We might come back to that as part of the
causes that we're talking about in a moment.
MS PICKERING: Sure.
DR WATERHOUSE: So that's the aged care numbers. And what
about the NDIS?
MS PICKERING: Unfortunately I probably don't have that
number to be able to share today across the district. Yes.
DR WATERHOUSE: Mr Shortis, do you have a sense from
Nepean Blue Mountains of the numbers that you are looking
at that are in hospital without needing acute care?
MR SHORTIS: I work in the community section so I'm only
aware of when they come to the community.
DR WATERHOUSE: Is it something you can speak to
anecdotally in terms of how frequently this is happening?
MR SHORTIS: Reports that I have is that it is
a significant hold-up, but I don't have the numbers. It's
not in my role.
DR WATERHOUSE: Mr Wakeling, are you able to speak for the
Illawarra in relation to these numbers?
MR WAKELING: Yes, thank you, Dr Waterhouse. As of
11 November, which was Monday, there were 38 NDIS patients
at Illawarra Shoalhaven that were suitable for discharge
but awaiting NDIS acceptance and support, and that's
40 per cent of our mental health bed base and 60 per cent
of our sub-acute bed base. The average length of stay,
once suitable for discharge, was 43 days, and at that point
in time, the amount of people awaiting NDIS and that length
of stay totalled 1,700 bed days.
As of Monday 11 November, patients awaiting
a residential aged care facility at Illawarra Shoalhaven
was 122. 15 per cent was in our ED accessible bed base and
the rest, 85 per cent, was in our sub-acute bed base. The
average length of stay, once suitable for discharge, was
19 days, and the volume and the length of stay totalled
3,500 bed days in Illawarra Shoalhaven. Thank you.

DR WATERHOUSE: Thank you.
Professor Potter, maybe if I could start with you, can
you outline what you see as the key causes of the delays in
being able to discharge aged care patients in particular,
given your background?
PROFESSOR POTTER: Okay. So in the last three years,
since the Royal Commission and COVID, we have lost 600 aged
care facility beds, permanently lost them from our
district, with no plans within the aged care sector to
rebuild these beds.
There's lots of reasons for that, which I can go into
if you want me to. So we've lost 600 beds, and that has
resulted in us having the numbers that Ben has already
spoken to waiting for placement.
Although he has given you the length of stay from
acceptance to placement to discharge, I would have to add
to that that specific groups of patients, in particular the
dementia patients with behavioural disturbance, can wait up
to a year for a bed, and there are no dementia-specific bed
vacancies at all in ISLHD aged care, and none of the
providers are proposing to build new dementia-specific
beds. So that's that particular issue for our patients
within hospital, waiting placements.
DR WATERHOUSE: When you say you've lost those beds, what
exactly do you mean by "lost"? Is it that the facilities
have closed or they can't --
PR0FESSOR POTTER: The providers have closed --
DR WATERHOUSE: Sorry?
PROFESSOR POTTER: Yes, the providers have closed the beds
permanently - for a variety of reasons to do with the Royal
Commission, a perception that these beds are not good
quality for patients, and the local council provisions on
what sorts of buildings can be built - a whole load of
different factors like that.
Also, during COVID, Illawarra Shoalhaven had a high
dependency on overseas nursing for aged care facilities
and, of course, there was a long period of time where we
couldn't have any overseas nurses coming in, so difficulty

staffing, difficulty making it work in terms of funding and
a reluctance and a poor perception of what going into
residential aged care means.
The majority of those 600 beds that have closed,
providers are considering opening things like retirement
villages for over 55s, not looking to provide the sort of
patient groups that we've got now waiting for placement.
DR WATERHOUSE: Do you find that patients --
THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry, I don't know whether Mr Wakeling
has his hand up, perhaps, to respond to that?
DR WATERHOUSE: Yes, Mr Wakeling?
MR WAKELING: It is, thank you, Commissioner. Thank you,
Dr Waterhouse. Just to support Professor Potter in regards
to the numbers on patients with severe behaviours or
aggression, at the moment at Wollongong Hospital, the
longest delay is 192 days, supporting Professor Potter's
"almost a year". The average at Wollongong is 19 days. In
our dementia-specific hospital where these patients are
awaiting residential aged care, Coledale hospital west wing
ward, which has 16 beds, their longest delay currently is
155 days, and the average wait there is 43 days, a
significant challenge for ISLHD. I just thought I would
add that to support Professor Potter. Thank you.
DR WATERHOUSE: Thank you.
Professor Potter do you find that there are delays in
actually having the patients assessed by ACAT teams or is
it really that that process is quite streamlined and it's
going from that point when they have been found suitable
for placement?
PROFESSOR POTTER: Look, we've done a lot of work looking
at this. Our ACAT teams are adhering to the KPIs for
hospitalised patients, which is within 40 hours of
referral. That's not to say there's not improvements that
could be made in that. There's often delays to making the
referral for aged care, and that comes down to the
underlying cause of the numbers. So within Illawarra
Shoalhaven, our population, we have a lot of people
retiring from cities to this area. Our proportion of frail
elderly is highest in New South Wales, in particular

Shoalhaven. We have approximately 5.7 residents who are
aged 80 or over, compared to 4.8 in New South Wales in
general, and that is really further exaggerated in
Shoalhaven.
So we've got this increasing need, we've got this
increasing dementia population, and at the same time, we're
losing and have lost the beds in the community funded by
the Commonwealth that we require to host those patients.
I think, going back to the delays to referring to
ACAT, that's because in Wollongong Hospital, for example,
which is our main tertiary hospital where we do most of our
admissions, we have a bed base of 21 patients for acute
geriatric medicine. We, at the moment, have a minimum of
60 patients in Wollongong Hospital at any one time. So
those other patients are scattered throughout surgical
wards, acute medical wards, where nursing staff and - also
we have gone from having 20 consultations to geriatric
medicine from other specialty teams, in the last two years,
to 60 a week, you know.
So basically, a lot of these patients are under teams
who do not have the expertise to manage them, do not have
the interest in that group either, and so that leads to
further delays in appropriate decisions being made.
DR WATERHOUSE: I'm going to come back to some of that if
I may. Can I just go, while we're still in the Illawarra,
to Ms Hawkins.
So do you find that patients - it's mainly in your
wards that you look after, it's mainly about placements,
obviously, but are there also patients waiting to be
transferred out for other types of care, such as
rehabilitation?
MS HAWKINS: Correct. So at the moment, between C7 east,
which is an aged care ward currently, a temporary aged care
ward, we currently have 15 patients admitted that are under
the care of a geriatrician; B3 east, there are 24, which is
our acute geriatric ward. So between the two wards, there
are currently 39 patients admitted under the care of
a geriatrician and there's nine --
DR WATERHOUSE: Just before you go on, can I clarify?

MS HAWKINS: Yes.
DR WATERHOUSE: When you say "under the care of
a geriatrician", does that mean they need acute care or
they just happen to be admitted under that person --
MS HAWKINS: They're admitted --
DR WATERHOUSE: -- but waiting transfer?
MS HAWKINS: Correct. So they're admitted under the care
of a geriatrician and then we've got 19 patients currently
under the care of a geriatrician that are outliers, and
then five of those patients are currently in the emergency
department.
In terms of C7 east aged care, we have five patients -
or actually, sorry, six patients - currently that are
awaiting Coledale hospital for nursing home placement. We
had one transferred this morning, which was awaiting GEM,
and the remaining patients are currently under an acute
care type, so they're still under the medical management of
the doctor.
DR WATERHOUSE: Thank you. Ms Pickering --
THE COMMISSIONER: Can I just ask, Ms Hawkins, were the
wards you're talking about - I should really know this, but
were they the wards that I had a site visit of? I think
they were, yes.
MS HAWKINS: Correct. So B3 east geriatrics is our
permanent 25-bed geriatric ward, and then C7 east is
currently utilised as a surge ward for geriatrics, so you
visited both those wards.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you for that.
MS HAWKINS: Just to add, in terms of the statistics of
those patients, so we currently have - I have the
statistics from yesterday, which was we had four patients
bed boarded to Coledale - the length of stay for our
longest length of stay was 212 days. On C7 east it was 34.
That patient was bed boarded since 1 May 2024. The next
patient is at 89 days' length of stay at Wollongong
Hospital, with a total length of stay on C7 east at
31 days. That patient was ready for step-down from

16 September 2024.
The next patient is at 111 days, as a hospital length
of stay. Length of stay on C7 east aged care is 36, and
has been bed boarded since 14 October. And our last
patient, as of the statistics for yesterday, 14 November,
was at 47 days with a total length of stay on our ward at
28 days. They were bed boarded since 2 October and ready
for transfer.
THE COMMISSIONER: My notes have a reference to "C7 west".
Did I just get my compass wrong or --
MS HAWKINS: Yes. C7 west is a different ward.
THE COMMISSIONER: That makes perfect sense, if you knew
me. The other ward I just wrote as "aged care ward". Is
that one of the wards you're talking about?
MS HAWKINS: Correct. So C7 east aged care is our surge
ward and then B3 east is our 25-bed permanent geriatric
ward.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
DR WATERHOUSE: If I can go to the Central Coast for
a moment, can you tell me, Ms Pickering, do you have
similar experience there in terms of some of those causes
of the delays?
MS PICKERING: Yes, we do. I think, as I started before,
the family choosing a facility is probably one of the big
areas that we find quite challenging and causing delays.
Families will often go and inspect a facility and decide
that, for whatever reason, it's not right for their loved
one, and so then they go and look at a second and a third
and sometimes a fourth.
Just to note that last month we did receive, via the
ministry, some guidance to support trying to facilitate and
empower families to make a decision with no more than two
choices. That's something that we'll be empowering and
working with our staff to work with families towards, with,
I guess, the conversation around, with the family, that if
they, on their second choice, are still not 100 per cent
satisfied, that they transfer with the view of looking, and
when the - once the facility that they're after is

available, that they can then transition across.
I guess the other challenges are those older people
with challenging behaviours and facilities, I guess,
accepting some of these older people into their residence.
Also at times we do have older people that have been
assessed that then do become acutely unwell in that period,
so then they become too unwell for transfer.
DR WATERHOUSE: Just on the family situation, are there
any financial incentives, perhaps, to let an elderly
patient just stay in hospital because it's going to cost
them money to be able to move them out?
MS PICKERING: Look, I think that's potentially a factor
that the family members consider. I think part of the
guidance that has come out, as I mentioned, last month from
the ministry also supports that care type change and
letting families know that there will potentially be a cost
attributed with an older person staying in an acute
facility that is no longer acute care.
DR WATERHOUSE: That is something that - I hear it has
come out last month, is that a new arrangement
altogether --
MS PICKERING: No.
DR WATERHOUSE: -- or is that something that just hasn't
been happening in a coordinated way perhaps?
MS PICKERING: It's not so much a new arrangement, it's
something that's, I guess, providing more guidance and
support from the ministry level for us to be able to enact
and empower with our staff.
DR WATERHOUSE: In terms of how it plays out in the ward
at Wyong, can you give an outline of the sorts of patients
that you have there waiting for long periods of time,
beyond the acute care they need, Ms Okulicz?
MS OKULICZ: Yes. It's mostly the behavioural patients,
the patients with challenging behaviours. We have to try
to medically treat them first and make sure that we can get
the - can we modify their behaviours using medications to
make them suitable because facilities won't take them

whilst they are having significantly challenging
behaviours.
We've also got issues regarding guardianship, those
delays as well. So if patients can't make decisions for
themselves or don't have capacity and are refusing to go,
then we need to go down the guardianship pathway and,
unfortunately, in their best interests take their
decision-making rights away from them, so it either gets
allocated to a family member or it can be to a guardian.
DR WATERHOUSE: How long does that guardianship process
take?
MS OKULICZ: It's significant. So we have to go through
all the assessments first of what the patient - treat the
patient first for what they're going through. Then we have
to assess their capacity, which can either be like
occupational therapist, social worker, neuro psych team,
geriatrician. It sometimes takes multiple people to do
those assessments.
Then once it is seen that they don't have capacity and
we're going place them against their wishes, we then have
to do all the letters and then that starts a seven-day
process where all the doctors, the social worker and
everyone who's involved write their letters.
Then that gets submitted to NCAT, the guardianship
board. Then they receive it and then they can take three
weeks before they give us a hearing date and then that
could be three to six weeks before we get then a hearing
date. Then we have the hearing, then it gets allocated,
and then the process of trying to find a suitable
residential aged care facility can start.
Then, once it's found, that goes back to the
guardianship board with everything submitted for their
recommendation for placement and then the guardian can then
take seven to 10 days to accept that place and put - do all
their paperwork. Then we can get given a transfer date,
which can be another week. So you're looking at up to,
like, three months from beginning to end for that patient.
DR WATERHOUSE: So to be clear, that is three months
starting from when they cease to need acute care in a
hospital?

MS OKULICZ: Correct.
DR WATERHOUSE: They are just in the ward?
MS OKULICZ: Yes.
DR WATERHOUSE: Are there ways that you can do some things
simultaneously? Can you be looking for an aged care
facility at the same time as they're going through the
process on the expectation --
MS OKULICZ: Yes, some families can. Some families are
willing to do that. But also it depends on what the
outcome is, because they may find a facility but they need
to work out is it an appropriate facility for them, because
we also have lots that need specific memory support units
going forward, and they have very limited beds, especially
on the Central Coast.
I've had one lady recently, that was only discharged
on Monday, she had been with me for about 150 days from
beginning to end, and then we finally found a facility, but
that was because the family were willing to consider other
areas and she actually got transferred to Belrose, in
Sydney, because we couldn't get any suitable bed on the
Central Coast.
DR WATERHOUSE: How many patients would you have at any
given time, going through that guardianship process?
MS OKULICZ: It can range from one to four, typically.
Yes. It's very variable. But I think four or five,
I think, is the most I've had at any one time.
DR WATERHOUSE: Mr Shortis, can I just ask you, from the
Nepean Blue Mountains' point of view, do you have
familiarity with the sorts of things that are keeping
patients in hospital, aged care patients or the NDIS
patients?
MR SHORTIS: Not enough to speak on, no.
DR WATERHOUSE: Did you want to make any comment at all in
relation to that?
MR SHORTIS: No, thank you.

DR WATERHOUSE: I think, Professor Potter, you wanted to
make a comment about this?
PROFESSOR POTTER: Yes, and just to say that in relation
to what you were saying about cost, which might be
a disincentive to families, there is a maintenance fee, so
when a patient is type changed to maintenance, which means
they no longer require acute or rehabilitation care,
they're ready to be discharged, they are charged a weekly
maintenance fee.
It's an absolute trivial amount compared to what a
family would have to pay for a bond for an aged care
facility. So you're talking around $20 a week compared to
a minimum of maybe a 500,000 bond. So there's obviously an
incentive, and particularly in Illawarra Shoalhaven, where
we cannot offer any dementia specific beds within the
region, so you're saying to a family, $20 a week versus
500,000, and you are going to have to travel to Sydney or
elsewhere. So it's a huge disadvantage.
DR WATERHOUSE: Am I right in understanding that the
amount that you can charge is set by --
PROFESSOR POTTER: Yes.
DR WATERHOUSE: Is that by the ministry or is that
a Commonwealth rate or how --
PROFESSOR POTTER: I think it's a Commonwealth rate in
negotiation with the ministry but it's an absolute
fraction. It's really --
DR WATERHOUSE: Yes, understood.
Ms Okulicz, could I --
THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry. Professor Potter, when you are
using the term "500,000 bond", you're referring to the RAD,
are you, the refundable deposit?
PROFESSOR POTTER: Yes, yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, thanks.
DR WATERHOUSE: They still have to come up with that in

the beginning, even if they're going to get it back in the
longer term, is that the point?
PROFESSOR POTTER: Yes, and if they get it back in the
longer term, they're not - you know, fees are going to be
taken out for how long they are in there. And again there
has been a whole load of speculation in the literature and
in the news stories about whether that's a fair and
equitable process or not, and I couldn't really comment,
but it's certainly debatable.
DR WATERHOUSE: Now, I'm aware that Mr Wakeling has his
hand up but Ms Okulicz also wanted to add something, I
think.
MS OKULICZ: Yes, in regards to the maintenance care, my
understanding for Central Coast, it was $67 a day,
potentially, that's charged for the maintenance period, but
there are ways families can avoid paying that as well.
There's a hardship form that they can submit as well. So
we can go through the maintenance process and they get
charged the daily rate, which is basically the same - like
a respite bed daily rate, but families can submit
a hardship form and not --
DR WATERHOUSE: And who decides whether that hardship
requirement is met?
MS OKULICZ: That is decided by the cashier, sorry, the
manager - sorry, I know her name but I don't know her role.
DR WATERHOUSE: Somebody in a management role within the
district?
MS OKULICZ: A management role within the clerks. They
work together with the finance department and determine if
it is hardship and they meet the criteria.
DR WATERHOUSE: Thank you.
Mr Wakeling, you wanted to add something?
MR WAKELING: Yes, thank you, Dr Waterhouse. Just in
support of the payment that Professor Potter raised and the
representative from Wyong, the average cost per bed day for
a maintenance patient at the Illawarra Shoalhaven is
$1,014, so the payment that those maintenance patients are

paying is, as Professor Potter said, a very fraction of the
cost of the LHD to run that bed.
DR WATERHOUSE: In other words, not only is it a fraction
of what they would be paying if they had the person placed
in an aged care facility, it's also a fraction of what it
is actually costing you to staff that bed?
MR WAKELING: Yes.
DR WATERHOUSE: Understood, thank you.
Can I just touch on whether or not, in the Central
Coast - do you know if you have lost beds in the same way
as Professor Potter was saying, with COVID and so on and
the Royal Commission, has there been the closure of a lot
of beds there?
MS PICKERING: I am aware that there have been some
facilities closed. I couldn't tell you how many beds, but
I don't think we've seen a large closure compared to what
others have.
DR WATERHOUSE: Mr Shortis, I think that one of the things
that you said when we met recently was you referred to the
fact that a lot of aged care patients may no longer be
seeing their general practitioners. Can you just expand on
why you feel that that's occurring or why you see that
happening?
MR SHORTIS: In Nepean Blue Mountains, one of the issues
that we have is there's not a huge number of GPs, so the
GPs are actually hard to get into, the clients themselves
can't attend, can't get an appointment, can't get one
within a timely fashion. There's just not the GPs
available to see there, and then combined with the mobility
issues of some of our clients and the lack of availability
of home visits, they just can't get to their GPs as often
as they would like.
DR WATERHOUSE: What is the flow-on effect from the point
of view of the district?
MR SHORTIS: From the point of view of the district, we
have patients who potentially could have been treated in
their home environment whose care isn't what's required,
and so they become more unwell and they are admitted to

facilities.
DR WATERHOUSE: Are there financial impediments to them
being able to see general practice as well or do they
mostly bulk bill them?
MR SHORTIS: My understanding is that most of the general
practices in the area I work in don't bulk bill the
majority of their clients. They do bulk bill based on an
individual assessment.
DR WATERHOUSE: Professor Potter, I was going to go to you
next, yes.
PROFESSOR POTTER: Just to say in regards to GPs and fees,
there's a huge financial disadvantage to general
practitioners to go into aged care facilities. They can
make, you know, far more for their practice by seeing
patients in five-, 10-minute appointments within their
surgery if the patients come to them, rather than going to
an aged care facility to see patients where they could be
there for many hours, they struggle to get nursing staff to
accompany them, the prescribing systems and electronic
writing systems are completely separate from their own.
It's not a very streamlined system at all and there's
a huge disadvantage to patients, and to GPs, for trying to
go in there. In the Illawarra Shoalhaven, we have a number
of facilities where the only GP input they can have is
telehealth from Victoria, which in reality, if you're
trying to assess a frail elderly patient with multiple
comorbidities who you've never met before, it really can't
be done very effectively by telehealth.
DR WATERHOUSE: In those circumstances where their only
general practitioner is a telehealth service from Victoria,
is there a lower threshold for just sending a person to
hospital if there's anything wrong with them?
PROFESSOR POTTER: There is often no alternative. You
now, in an acute crisis, you'll only be able to get the
telehealth person at certain times, it's all very, you
know, office hours, and so they feel - I think, you know,
in terms of the aged care facilities, they feel as if they
have no alternative. We have put in place, and we're
trying to expand, a number of strategies to support the
facilities, which we can talk about later if you wish.

DR WATERHOUSE: One thing I wanted to ask, is it
a requirement, in order to be able to go into a residential
aged care facility that you must have a nominated general
